items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1995-08-29
items.q: showed pictures of Conk Basie, Duke Ellington, Jimmy Liggins, Billy Eckstein, Joe Lewis. Image factors that blacks could look up to. Sure. But they had never seen these people. They've only rarely heard them.

ctx.x: All right, well. I'm sorry. Let me ask a question. I had a broader question I was going to get back to WMR. Why do you think, finally, at this point in time, that there is black radio, finally? All right.

All right. You've got to remember. Now, we started talking about the black newspapers. The three black newspapers we had, the Informer Sentinel, La Courier, and Louisiana Wheeler, showed pictures of Conk Basie, Duke Ellington, Jimmy Liggins, Billy Eckstein, Joe Lewis. Image factors that blacks could look up to. Sure. But they had never seen these people. They've only rarely heard them. See, you didn't have jukeboxes. You had jukeboxes, but they were just beginning to highlight the black intelligentsia and…
But you met a lot of women, huh, Tex?

items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1996-01-10
items.q: I think that's where our first, Jimmy Liggins played a hucklebuck

ctx.x: Right, yeah, January the 10th, 1996, Real Number 3 with Tech Stevens.

And, you know, as we were saying, Ted, we were talking about writing columns and so forth, about knowing people, about getting involved, having the right kind of connection, so that you could get into the structure of putting something together to inform in a newspaper, because a lot of people call newspaper an organ. It's an organ of information. That's what a newspaper is. See, and I highlight, I was talking about Charlie Rosenthal over in Orange, Texas, who was a good friend of Frank Pannier. Both of them were…
Her daddy would have known, though.
